title: Rubik's cube, layer by layer
lead: A beginner's method: about seven algorithms, one layer at a time. It takes more moves than the computer but anyone can learn it.
intro: Letters name the face to turn clockwise as you look at it: U up, D down, R right, L left, F front, B back. An apostrophe means counter-clockwise, and a 2 means a half turn.
steps: White cross

Put white on top and make a plus sign, with each white edge's other colour matching its side centre. Do this by intuition: bring an edge to the layer beneath, line up its side colour, then turn it up.
White corners
Hold a white corner under where it belongs, then repeat the moves until it drops in correctly.
R U R' U'
Middle layer
Turn the cube white-side down. Find a top edge with no yellow, and match its front colour to a centre. To send it to the right use the first sequence, and to the left use the second.
U R U' R' U' F' U F|U' L' U L U F U' F'
Yellow cross
Look at the top. A dot, an L shape or a line of yellow edges becomes a cross when you repeat this sequence. Hold an L at the back-left, or a line horizontally.
F R U R' U' F'
Line up the yellow edges
Turn the top until at least two edges match their sides. Hold a matching edge at the back and another on the right, then use this sequence.
R U R' U R U2 R'
Place the yellow corners
Find a corner already in the right place, hold it at the front-right, and repeat until all four are in place.
U R U' L' U R' U' L
Twist the last corners

Hold an unsolved corner at the front-right. Repeat these moves until it is yellow on top, then turn only the top layer to bring the next one there. The lower layers look scrambled midway and fix themselves.
R' D' R D
tip: Learn one stage at a time, and practise with the type-your-moves box on the cube page.

title: Sudoku by logic
intro: Each row, column and 3×3 box must hold 1 to 9 exactly once.
steps: Scan for hidden singles
Pick a digit and check each box. If only one cell in the box can hold it, it goes there.
Naked singles
Pick an empty cell and rule out digits in its row, column and box. If one candidate remains, write it in.
Pencil marks
On harder puzzles, write small candidates in each cell. Update them every time you place a digit.
Pairs
If two cells in a unit share the same two candidates, those digits must go in those cells, so remove them from the rest of the unit.
Pointing candidates
If a digit's candidates within a box all sit in one row, that digit can be removed from the rest of that row outside the box.
X-wing
If a digit appears in exactly two cells in each of two rows, and those cells share the same two columns, remove it from elsewhere in those columns.
tip: When stuck, go back to scanning: new placements often open easy singles.

title: Lights Out: chase the lights
lead: A method that solves any solvable 5×5 board.
intro: Pressing a light toggles it and its four neighbours. Order never matters, and pressing twice cancels out.
steps: Chase downward
Working down from the top row, for each light that is on, press the light directly below it. This clears each row in turn.
Read the bottom row
Only the bottom row can now be lit. Look up its pattern in the table below.
Press the top row
Press the top-row positions given in the table.
Chase again
Repeat the downward chase. The board goes dark.
tip: 1 means lit or pressed, reading from left to right.

title: Mastermind: think like a cryptanalyst
lead: Every answer eliminates possible codes, so choose guesses that split the remaining codes evenly.
intro: There are 1,296 possible codes with four pegs and six colours.
steps: Open with two pairs
A guess like red red blue blue tells you more than four different colours or a single repeated colour.
Add up the pegs
The total of black and white pegs tells you how many of those colours are in the code.
Make every guess consistent
Only guess codes that could still be right, given all earlier feedback.
Change a little at a time
When several codes remain, change only part of the guess, so the feedback is easier to interpret.
tip: This is frequency analysis in miniature: learn what is present first, then where.

title: Sliding tiles
lead: Solve in pieces and never disturb finished pieces.
intro: Think of it as moving the empty space around.
steps: Top row first
Bring 1 and 2 into place. For the last tile of a row, tuck the tile just below its slot, then rotate it in.
Left column next
Solve the first column the same way, and treat it as finished.
Finish the 2×2
The remaining block rotates like a ring. Cycle tiles around until they line up.
tip: Half of all random arrangements cannot be solved. Boards in this app always can.

title: Tower of Hanoi
lead: A simple rhythm that never fails.
intro: Move one disc at a time, and never put a larger disc on a smaller one.
steps: Move the smallest disc every other turn
Always move it in the same circular direction. With an even number of discs, go first to the middle peg; with an odd number, go to the far peg.
On other turns
Make the only legal move that does not involve the smallest disc.
Think recursively
To move n discs, move n−1 out of the way, move the largest, then move the n−1 back on top.

title: N-Queens
lead: Place row by row, and retreat on conflict.
intro: No two queens may share a row, column or diagonal.
steps: One queen per row
Place a queen in the next row, in the first safe column.
Mark attacks
Cover every column and diagonal it attacks.
Retreat
If a row has no safe square, go back one row and move that queen to its next safe square.
tip: This backtracking is the same idea used to solve sudoku by computer.

title: Knight's Tour
lead: One rule of thumb does nearly all the work.
intro: A knight moves two squares in one direction and one in the other, and must visit each square once.
steps: Warnsdorff's rule
From your square, look at each possible next move. Count how many onward moves each would have, and go to the one with the fewest.
Why it works
Squares near edges have few entrances, so using them early avoids stranding them.
tip: Corners are the most at risk, so favour them whenever you can.

title: Nonograms
lead: Use overlap and logic, line by line.
intro: Clues give the lengths of runs of filled cells, in order, with at least one gap between runs.
steps: Overlap
Slide a run as far left and as far right as it can go. Any cell covered in both positions must be filled.
Mark blanks
When a line's clues are all placed, cross off its remaining cells.
Use edges
A filled cell near an edge can force a run to start there.
Alternate rows and columns
Each new mark can unlock a line in the other direction.
tip: Start with the longest clues, which have the most overlap.

title: Break a substitution cipher by hand
lead: The method al-Kindi described, still satisfying with a pencil.
intro: Each letter has been replaced by one other letter throughout the message.
steps: Count the letters
The most common letters probably stand for E, T, A and O in English.
Look for short words
One-letter words are usually A or I. A common three-letter word is often THE or AND.
Use patterns
A word such as XYZZYX has its repeated letters in a telling pattern. Double letters are often LL, EE, SS or OO.
Build the key
Write your guesses above the ciphertext in pencil, and let partial words suggest the next letter.
Check it reads
Keep going until the whole text makes sense. If a guess forces nonsense, undo it.
tip: Try the Challenge page for practice ciphers, and the Workbench for letter counts.
